extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of mythology and comparative religion; introductory-level scholars
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory textbook chapter that defines key terms (myth, folklore, folk-tale, legend) and surveys major conceptual categories and developmental processes in mythic studies (animism, fetishism, totemism, polytheism, monotheism, etc.), offering examples and interpretive guidance for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A myth is an account of the deeds of a god or supernatural being, usually expressed in terms of primitive thought; an attempt to explain the relations of man to the universe and often having a predominantly religious value; may explain the origin of social organization, customs, or environmental peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myths are narrative traditions that explain cosmic, social, or ritual phenomena; when classifying a story as myth, look for a god/demigod or supernatural explanatory function rather than merely aesthetic or local-historical content. Examples and analogies are used throughout to show how myths explain natural and social features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythology (definition / scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythology implies (a) the mythic system of any race and (b) the investigation of myth; used both for the body of myths and the scholarly study of myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term to refer either to a people's collective myths (their mythic system) or to the academic discipline studying myths. The book treats mythology as the science of myths distinct from but overlapping comparative religion and folklore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folklore (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Folklore means the study of survivals of early custom, belief, narrative, and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish folklore (survivals, fragments, practices in modern or semi-civilized settings) from living primitive mythology; in analysis, determine whether materials are survivals or part of an active mythic system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk-tale (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A folk-tale is a primitive tale (a) of mythical origin or (b) of purely narrative or æsthetic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a narrative as folk-tale when its primary value is narrative/aesthetic or when it derives from older mythic materials but functions as a tale rather than an explicitly religious explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legend (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legend is a story, generally of real places and often (though not necessarily) of real persons, handed down by 'tradition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legends tend to be localized and historically anchored; distinguish legends from myths by the centering on real places/people rather than supernatural explanatory aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Mythology vs Folklore
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythology studies primitive or early forms of religion while they were living faiths; folklore studies primitive religion and customs as survivals still practised among uncultured or semi-cultured groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scholarly classification, determine whether a narrative represents a living religious belief (myth) or a fragment/survival in a later population (folklore). Examples: speaking of 'folklore of England' is appropriate for survivals, while calling living tribal beliefs 'folklore' can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of mythology is the investigation and explanation of myths or tales relating to the early religious and scientific experiences of mankind; it throws light upon material, methods, and progress of primitive religion and science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat myths as sources for understanding primitive thought, religion, and early scientific attempts; analysis should emphasize explanatory intent (why a myth was told) and its informational value about past beliefs and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth and religion relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythology overlaps comparative religion; comparative religion is a branch of religious science, while mythology deals specifically with myths (and under 'comparative mythology' compares myths of different races). Mythology is thus part of religious science but has its own focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When situating a study, clarify whether emphasis is on doctrinal/religious analysis (comparative religion) or on mythic narratives and their explanations (mythology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Savage element in myth (primitive/barbaric residues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths frequently retain 'savage' or 'barbaric' elements—irrational, coarse, or violent motifs—reflecting primitive mental attitudes; later poets/priests often cleanse and refine myths, obscuring original meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In interpretation, look for elements that reflect earlier, less 'civilized' outlooks (e.g., cannibalism motifs, animal disguises, fetishism). Consider historical processes of refinement by elite agents and beware of interpreting later sanitized versions as original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as primitive science
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths often function as early, 'savage' science—attempts to explain natural phenomena, origins, and customs; they arise to answer 'the reason why' questions and thus reflect an early scientific impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze myths for explanatory content about natural phenomena, cosmology, origins of species/customs; treat mythic explanations as evidence that such questions were posed and that myth served cognitive functions analogous to science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animism (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animism: the belief that everything has a soul or personality; regarded as the earliest recognized phase of religious experience and the source of many animistic myths (talking animals, metamorphoses, spirit-journeys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify animistic traces by narratives featuring separable souls (souls as birds/bees), spirit-journeys, or metamorphosis. Consider animism as a 'fossil faith'—a theoretical stage inferred from surviving motifs and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-animistic religion / Supernaturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesized earlier phase (supernaturalism) in which awe of mysterious 'powers' precedes full animistic ideas of spirits; objects inspiring awe may be treated as powers without explicit spirit conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing developmental sequences, consider Marett's proposal that emotion/awe ('supernaturalism') may precede ideation of spirits; look for cultic behaviors or reverence toward phenomena lacking explicit personified spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fetishism (definition and distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fetishism: belief in objects (natural or artificial) regarded as possessed by spirit, consciousness, or magic power (a 'favourite' object or charm). Distinct from a god: a fetish is subservient to an owner/tribe and may develop into a god by long service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify fetishistic elements by attention to objects treated as inhabiting spirits (stones, bones, bundles); note rituals (wrapping, offerings), owner-control dynamics, and transitional development from fetish to idol/god. Examples: flint-stone as thunder emblem (Brounger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Totemism (definition and social role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Totemism: animal, plant, or inanimate object traditionally connected with a social group that may claim descent or relationship to the totem; magico-religious bonds restrain consumption and impose ceremonial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize totemism where communities preserve prohibitions (not eating the totem), ritual kinship, or tribal names/symbols derived from animals/plants. Use ethnographic parallels (Iroquois, Egyptian animal-headed gods) to interpret totemic traces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polytheism (development and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polytheism: condition of many gods, often arranged hierarchically mirroring social polity; arises by differentiation, absorption, or personalization of attributes into separate deities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how gods multiply or specialize (e.g., Egyptian Horus variants), how local cults are integrated into pantheons, and how social/political processes (conquest, migration, priestly influence) shape pantheon structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotheism (emergence and characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotheism: worship of one god which may arise from polytheism by absorption, conquest, priestly enterprise, or moral/religious development; such gods often possess rights like pardoning sin and represent an exalted religious outlook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical analysis, consider political and moral factors driving monotheism, and identify functions monotheistic systems serve (moral authority, centralized cult).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fetish-to-god developmental pathway
rubrics_metrics.description: A fetish (an object infused with spirit) may, through prolonged veneration and social ritual, develop into a higher-status deity or 'godling'—the line between fetish, idol, and god can be slender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating material culture and cult practice, map evidence of increasing communal veneration (temple placement, wrapping in cloth, ritual use) as indicators of fetish elevation toward godhood. Examples: local stones becoming objects of worship and cult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear definitions and coordinated review
rubrics_metrics.description: A major drawback in mythology has been lack of accepted definitions and absence of an historical/philosophical review presented on popular lines to coordinate research results; clear working definitions are necessary for the science to expand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should adopt precise working definitions (as the author proposes) and aim for syntheses that coordinate research findings; comparative tables and methodical definitions help students avoid conceptual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly method: eclecticism and use of collected evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The author advocates an eclectic method—embracing the best elements of various theories—illustrating theories as far as possible with myths personally collected or directly observed rather than relying solely on armchair compilations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer integrating insights from multiple theoretical approaches and grounding interpretations in primary collected data and comparative examples; be cautious of single-theory pride and over-reliance on untested speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution: later refinement obscures originals
rubrics_metrics.description: As peoples civilize, myths are often refined or cleansed by priests, poets, or philosophers, which can obscure original meanings; later forms may be poor guides to primitive origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing origins, account for processes of literary/priestly revision and treat later classical versions analytically—seek comparative, ethnographic, or archaeological corroboration for primitive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative and ethnographic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative tables and cross-cultural examples are essential tools for illustrating theories and demonstrating universal patterns in myth development (e.g., swallowing/disgorging motifs, stone worship, rain charms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ wide-ranging cross-cultural data to test hypotheses about mythic motifs and processes; the author emphasizes collecting examples personally and consulting a variety of authorities to support interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tylor's claim: laws of mythic growth/regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths display regularity of development attributable to laws of growth rather than motiveless fancy; these laws are practically universal in their application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theoretical work, look for regular developmental patterns and propose testable principles explaining motif diffusion and morphological changes; use comparative evidence to substantiate claims of regularity.
